lead: Proof of Stake is a consensus rule where validators lock the chain's own coin and are chosen to propose blocks in proportion to that locked amount. It exists because Proof of Work spends electricity to make block production costly. In PoS the cost is capital at risk: a validator's deposit can be destroyed if it cheats. Ethereum switched from PoW to PoS in 2022, and many newer chains use PoS or its delegated form.
prereq: You need: 3.3 for proof-based consensus and Sybil resistance, and Unit 2 for digital signatures.

blocks.text: The scarce resource in Proof of Stake is the native coin, not electricity. A node that wants to validate sends a special transaction that locks a deposit called its stake. The locked coins stay in the protocol and cannot be spent while the validator is active. The set of validators and their stakes is public, so every node can compute the same selection odds.

blocks.where: P(i) is the chance validator i proposes the next block; s_i is its stake in coins; S = Σ s_j is the total staked coins over all active validators.

blocks.text: Selection can be stake-weighted, coin-age-based, or nearly random with equal chance. Stake-weighted selection is common: pick a random point in the total stake and see whose interval it falls in. Coin-age selection multiplies stake by time unspent to reward long holders, but it can encourage going offline and returning. Pure random selection treats every validator equally, which needs another rule to stop Sybil identities.

items: Deposit the native coin into the staking contract and wait for activation.
When selected, propose exactly one block at that height.
Attest to other validators' blocks to support the chain.
Earn rewards in proportion to stake and participation.
If the validator signs two different blocks at the same height, slashing destroys part of the stake and removes it.

blocks.text: The nothing-at-stake problem appears when signing many competing forks costs nothing. A validator could vote on every branch and collect rewards whichever wins. PoS answers with slashing: a validator that signs two different blocks at the same height, or two conflicting attestations, loses part of its stake, and the protocol removes it. The evidence is the two signed messages, so any node can prove the offence.

A checkpoint is a block that the protocol treats as final after enough validators attest. Finality means the block cannot be reverted without validators losing large deposits. Without checkpoints, PoS gives probabilistic settlement: more confirmations means lower reorg chance. With checkpoints, in Casper-style designs a checkpoint is first justified, then finalised one epoch later, so finality takes two epochs.

The long-range attack uses old validator keys to build a different history from an early point. A new node cannot tell which history is real by stake alone. Checkpoints and weak subjectivity solve this: a new node trusts a recent checkpoint from a known source, and old keys below the checkpoint cannot rewrite it.
In Delegated Proof of Stake, token holders vote for a small set of block producers. Those producers take turns making blocks; voters can remove them by re-voting.

items: Advantage: low energy use, because there is no hash race.
Advantage: cheap hardware, since a normal server or cloud VM can validate.
Advantage: faster finality, because checkpoints can finalize in seconds or a few slots.
Disadvantage: rich get richer, as rewards add to the largest stakes.
Disadvantage: cartel risk: a few large stakers, or a small producer set, can coordinate to control block production.
Disadvantage: security needs a large honest share of stake: above 50% an attacker can dominate block choice and censor, and finality rules usually need about two thirds of stake attesting.

figure.caption: Four validators hold 500, 300, 150 and 50 tokens out of 1000. A's 50% chance is the largest; B's 30% is shown before its later penalty.

spec.title: Chance to propose is stake / total stake
spec.aria: Four validators hold different stakes, and each one's chance of being chosen to propose a block equals its share of the total stake.

examples.question: Four validators A, B, C and D lock 500, 300, 150 and 50 tokens. Total stake is 1000 tokens. (a) Find each validator's chance of proposing the next block. (b) In 100 blocks, how many blocks should each propose on average? (c) Suppose this chain applies a 5% penalty without ejection (some PoS designs do this). B double-signs and pays the penalty. Find the penalty amount, B's new stake, B's new chance using the old total for comparison, and B's new chance after the destroyed tokens leave the total.
steps: Expected blocks in 100 = chance × 100: A gets 50, B gets 30, C gets 15, D gets 5 blocks.
Penalty on B = 5% × 300 = 0.05 × 300 = 15 tokens. B's new stake = 300 − 15 = 285 tokens.
Using the old total, B's chance = 285 ÷ 1000 = 0.285 = 28.5%. After the 15 destroyed tokens leave the total, new total = 1000 − 15 = 985 tokens. Final chance = 285 ÷ 985 = 0.28934 = 28.93%.
examples.answer: A, B, C and D have 50%, 30%, 15% and 5%; expected blocks are 50, 30, 15 and 5. B pays 15 tokens, falls to 285, shows 28.5% of the old total, and 28.93% after the total falls to 985 tokens.
examples.check:
stakes = [500, 300, 150, 50]
total = sum(stakes)
for s in stakes:
    print(int(s * 100 / total))
slash = 0.05 * stakes[1]
print(int(slash))
new_b = stakes[1] - slash
print(int(new_b))
print(new_b / total * 100)
new_total = total - slash
print(round(new_b / new_total * 100, 2))

traps: PoS does not remove all attacks. A holder above 50% of stake can still reorganise or censor blocks.
Slashing is not a normal transaction fee. It destroys part of the stake and removes the validator.
Chance is stake ÷ total stake, not stake ÷ 100 or stake ÷ initial supply. The denominator changes when slashed coins are destroyed.
Nothing-at-stake is answered by slashing and checkpoints, not by faster hardware or more confirmations alone.
Probabilistic settlement and checkpoint finality are different. A block is final only when the protocol's checkpoint rule says so.

quiz.q: What is a validator's stake in Proof of Stake?
quiz.a: Coins locked by the validator in the protocol as a deposit. The stake can be slashed if the validator misbehaves.

quiz.q: Why does Proof of Stake use slashing?
quiz.a: Slashing makes misbehaviour costly. If a validator signs two different blocks at the same height, or two conflicting attestations, part of its locked stake is destroyed and it is removed. This answers the nothing-at-stake problem.

quiz.q: Validators hold 400, 300, 200 and 100 tokens, total 1000. What is the third validator's chance of proposing the next block, and its expected blocks in 50 blocks?
Why is the nothing-at-stake problem less direct in Proof of Work?
quiz.a: In PoW, extending two competing forks needs hash power on both. A miner cannot give full hash power to both branches at once, so voting on many forks has an opportunity cost. In early PoS, signing many forks had no comparable cost.

quiz.q: How does a checkpoint limit a long-range attack?
quiz.a: A checkpoint is treated as final. Old validator keys cannot rewrite history below it without breaking finality. A new node trusts a recent checkpoint, so an attacker cannot build a competing chain from an early point and present it as valid.

quiz.q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of Proof of Stake.
quiz.a: Advantage: low energy use, because there is no hash race. Disadvantage: large stakeholders have more influence, so the rich-get-richer effect and cartel risk need attention.

quiz.q: Suppose this chain applies a penalty without ejection (some PoS designs do this). A validator has 240 tokens out of a total 800. It pays a 25-token penalty. Find its new stake, its chance using the old total, and its chance after the destroyed tokens leave the total.
quiz.a: New stake = 240 − 25 = 215 tokens. Old-total chance = 215 ÷ 800 = 26.875%. New total = 800 − 25 = 775. Final chance = 215 ÷ 775 = 0.2774 = 27.74%.

quiz.q: State Delegated Proof of Stake in one sentence.
quiz.a: Token holders vote for a small set of block producers, and those producers take turns making blocks while voters can replace them.

beyond: Not for the exam. Ethereum's PoS uses validator queues, attestation committees and a finality gadget; read the beacon chain specification next. Staking pools and liquid staking tokens are a large industry, and they raise centralisation questions. Researchers work on accountable safety, weak subjectivity checkpoints and single-slot finality. Search terms: Casper FFG, slashing condition, weak subjectivity, delegated proof of stake.
